subject_line: Jack and Bet, and a South London street that keeps changing
email_body:
Dear Sarah,

Jack & Bet stays with an octogenarian couple whose marriage has outlasted almost everything around them, while their corner of South London shifts under their feet. Before the Fire, too, grew out of a specific place: north Manchester in the 2011 riots. For a Spotlight, I would love to ask how you find a street or neighbourhood that can carry a whole novel.

subject_line: From Rodinsky's Room to The Prince of Whitechapel
email_body:
Dear Rachel,

Your writing keeps returning to East London and to what people leave behind, from Rodinsky's Room and On Brick Lane to The Prince of Whitechapel, with its rescued archive. Estuary took that attention out along the Thames to the sea. You also co-direct the Centre for Place Writing at Manchester Met. For a Spotlight, I would love to ask how you decide when an archive or a street has become a book.

subject_line: Glass, twice over: from The Glass Delusion to Water & Glass
email_body:
Dear Abi,

Glass seems to follow you across forms: The Glass Delusion, the Salt collection that won a Somerset Maugham Award, and then Water & Glass, a novel that takes on climate change. I was curious whether that echo was deliberate, and how moving from poems to a full-length dystopian story changed the way you handle a single image. With The Headland also on your list, that seems a natural thread for a Spotlight.

subject_line: Writing between South Africa and Leeds in Thin Slices
email_body:
Dear Caitlin,

Thin Slices moves between South Africa and the UK and was billed at its Leeds launch as a set of experiments in poetry, psychology and science. Since then you have co-written The Smell of Blood and Other Stories with Kharys Ateh Laue for Karavan Press. For a Spotlight, I would love to ask what changes when you share a story collection with another writer, and whether the experimental habits of Thin Slices carried over into prose.

subject_line: Malcolm Gandy, Bill's Mother and writing the Potteries
email_body:
Dear Lisa,

Sitting Ducks puts a mother and son in Stoke-on-Trent up against the system and a predatory landlord, Malcolm Gandy, to keep their council home, and the title of It's Gone Dark over Bill's Mother's carries the same unmistakable local voice. With Pondweed following from Myriad, I would love to ask in a Spotlight how the Potteries' speech finds its way onto the page, and what you protect when you write about a place that is often written about from outside.

subject_line: The Star Carr frontlet on the cover of Maskwork
email_body:
Dear Gregory,

The cover of Maskwork carries the Mesolithic red-deer frontlet from Star Carr, and the poems take that object seriously: the mask as a way of becoming, seeing and knowing, binding people to their ecological surroundings. Zaffar Kunial placed the book in the land of Beorma, which made me wonder how Birmingham and that deep prehistoric past sit together for you. That question, and the collection's Laurel Prize longlisting, could anchor a short Spotlight.

Dear Philip,

Relocating Dante's Purgatorio to Mersea Island is a wonderfully specific choice, and it seems to continue what you began with your Inferno and with Shakespeare's Sonnets: taking a canonical text and making it answer to a particular place and moment. For a Spotlight, I would love to ask what Mersea gave the mountain of Purgatory that another setting could not, and how you decide how far a version can travel from its source before it becomes something new.

Dear James,

Father Myself, your second collection from Nine Arches, comes out of the weeks around your father's death in 2022, and it follows Manatomy, which looked at how nature, nurture, pop culture and politics shaped you. You also write for EastEnders and for the stage, from Jab to Rubber Ring. For a Spotlight, I would be interested in how you decide whether something becomes a poem, a play or a scene, and how writing so close to grief sat alongside that work.

email_body:
Dear Jane,

A User's Guide to Make-Believe looks ahead to a near future, while your story 'In Yon Green Hill to Dwell', which won The Fiction Desk's ghost story competition, reaches back towards something much older and stranger. I also saw that you have been gathering uncanny short stories. For a Spotlight, I would love to ask how speculative technology and the folkloric uncanny sit side by side in your imagination, and whether your work as a visual artist shapes either.

subject_line: Child Ballad, Stretto and a woman between the castle walls
email_body:
Dear David,

Child Ballad, your sixth collection, was a Sunday Times Poetry Book of the Year. Alongside the poems there is Stretto, and I read that you are now writing a novel about a woman who lives between the walls of a Scottish castle and believes she is Bonnie Prince Charlie. For a Spotlight, I would love to ask what fiction lets you do that a poem will not, and how the north-east of Scotland has worked its way into both.

subject_line: Joyce, the Volta and Paradise House
email_body:
Dear Paul,

Paradise House imagines a life for James Joyce in which the Volta, Ireland's first cinema, actually succeeded. It is a tempting counterfactual, and it sits interestingly beside Jamais Vu, shortlisted for the Farmgate National Poetry Book Award, and the novels you co-write as Karen Perry. For a Spotlight, I would love to ask what drew you to that particular Joyce, and how moving between poetry, solo fiction and collaborative thrillers changes the way you work.

subject_line: Privilege and poverty in All The Money In The World
email_body:
Dear Sarah,

All The Money In The World takes on privilege, educational disadvantage, poverty and identity, which is a lot to hand a young reader, and The Shark and the Scar followed soon after. As a professor at the University of Limerick, you spend your days thinking about education too. For a Spotlight, I would love to ask how that work feeds your fiction for young people, and what it is like to know your novels are read in sixteen languages.

subject_line: Dieffenbach, Djuna and the shape of a novel in episodes
email_body:
Dear Thom,

The Naturalist followed Ernst Dieffenbach on his 1839 expedition to New Zealand, and The Salted Air turned to Djuna, grieving and drawn to her partner's married brother, in a scrapbook of short chapters. I also noticed your work as Thomas Gough in Conjunctions, and a novel built from short, self-contained episodes. For a Spotlight, I would love to ask how that fragmentary form has developed since The Salted Air, and how teaching at Massey in Palmerston North shapes it.

Dear Paula,

Hiwa gathers twenty-seven writers working in English or te reo Māori, and it follows A Clear Dawn, which you co-edited with Alison Wong as the first anthology of Asian New Zealand writing. subject_line: Tama the magpie and a Central Otago farm
email_body:
Dear Catherine,

Handing The Axeman's Carnival to Tama, a magpie raised by Marnie on the high-country farm she shares with Rob, is such a bold choice of narrator, and it made you the first writer to win the Jann Medlicott Acorn Prize twice, after The Wish Child. For a Spotlight, I would love to ask how you found Tama's voice, and whether teaching writing at Waikato has changed how you think about who gets to tell a story.
